## Load the data

```{r}
# make sure to use the VolleyBuffs repo as the working directory for the following chunks or whatever works best on ur computer
# Try this maybe?
repo_root <- if (dir.exists("VolleyBuffs/R")) "VolleyBuffs" else "."
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = normalizePath(repo_root))
library(e1071)
```

```{r}
# Run the wrangling script to have all the whatnot needed. All the wrangling and cleaning is handled in that script not in here
source("R/make_splits.R")
```

The script creates two data frames containing the same rally observations:
`score_only` and `score_plus_skills`. These include identifiers and the outcome,
so we should not pass every column directly to the models.

It also creates numeric predictor matrices: `x_score` and `x_skills`.
The separate factor `y` contains the home team's (which is CU) eventual `loss` or `win`.
The starting skill matrix uses cumulative counts and the rates remain available in
the larger data frame for later selection and preprocessing.

## Preparing the training/test split

```{r,echo=FALSE,message=FALSE}
# wanna have match IDs alongside the inputs so entire matches stay together
# don't wanna have these as predictors as they identify matches, not performance
match_ids <- score_plus_skills$match_id
```


```{r}
set.seed(303) # favorite seed and makes it reproducible

# List each match once, in a consistent order
matches <- sort(unique(match_ids))

# Setting aside 20% of matches for testing for an 80/20 training/testing split
test_matches <- sample(
  matches,
  size = ceiling(0.20 * length(matches))
)

# We'll identify the rows being used for the testing
# both predictor matrices have exactly the same row order for consistency
is_test <- match_ids %in% test_matches

# score-only inputs.
x_score_train <- x_score[!is_test, , drop = FALSE]
x_score_test  <- x_score[is_test, , drop = FALSE]

# score-plus-skills inputs will also use the same ids as score only
x_skills_train <- x_skills[!is_test, , drop = FALSE]
x_skills_test  <- x_skills[is_test, , drop = FALSE]

# making sure to pick the ids that aren't part of the testing
y_train <- y[!is_test]
y_test  <- y[is_test]
```


## Model Creation
Here we establish each model and will tune soon

```{r}
# The seed also makes the probability-estimation step reproducible for the future
set.seed(4640)
# This is the score only model
svm_score <- svm(
  x = x_score_train,        # this uses the training predictors
  y = y_train,              # the y training has the known win/loss outcome
  type = "C-classification",
  kernel = "radial",         # RBF is a good standard
  cost = 5,                  # will tune this later
  gamma = 1 / ncol(x_score_train), # This the default, will tune later.
  probability = TRUE,       # estimating probabilities too
  scale = TRUE              # this is for creating a standardization for each predictor rather than having outliers overpowering relationships
)

# No we are fitting the score-plus-skills model with same training as the previous but with skills
set.seed(4640)
svm_skills <- svm(
  x = x_skills_train,
  y = y_train,              # Ensuring we use the same outcomes and training observations as to not compare different things
  type = "C-classification",
  kernel = "radial",
  cost = 5,
  gamma = 1 / ncol(x_skills_train), # Same default rule, different number of inputs
  probability = TRUE,
  scale = TRUE
)

# this will see how the models predicted
pred_score <- predict(svm_score, newdata = x_score_test, probability = TRUE)
pred_skills <- predict(svm_skills, newdata = x_skills_test, probability = TRUE)

# Confusing mat or something
table(Actual = y_test, Predicted = pred_score)
table(Actual = y_test, Predicted = pred_skills)

# Fraction of the test set snapshot accurately identified
mean(pred_score == y_test)
mean(pred_skills == y_test) # Compare these runs, but this is not the final tuned result
```





## Comparing probabilities

The accuracy above weights each rally equally. Here I average within each set
first, so a longer set doesn't dominate the comparison. Lower Brier score and
log loss are better. These probabilities do not require a classification threshold.

```{r}
# Get the probability of a HOME win by class name, not column position.
p_score <- attr(pred_score, "probabilities")[, "win"]
p_skills <- attr(pred_skills, "probabilities")[, "win"]

# Keep the same held-out set identifiers for both models.
results <- score_only[is_test, c("match_id", "set_number")] |>
  mutate(actual_win = as.integer(y_test == "win"),
         score_only = p_score, score_plus_skills = p_skills) |>
  pivot_longer(c(score_only, score_plus_skills),
               names_to = "model", values_to = "probability") |>
  mutate(brier = (probability - actual_win)^2,
         # Avoid taking log(0) for probabilities at the extremes.
         clipped = pmin(pmax(probability, 1e-8), 1 - 1e-8),
         log_loss = -(actual_win * log(clipped) +
                        (1 - actual_win) * log(1 - clipped)))

model_comparison <- results |>
  group_by(model, match_id, set_number) |>
  summarise(brier = mean(brier), log_loss = mean(log_loss), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(model) |>
  summarise(test_sets = n(), brier = mean(brier), log_loss = mean(log_loss),
            .groups = "drop")
model_comparison
```

These are preliminary comparisons. Both models use cost 5 and the default gamma
rule (1 divided by the number of inputs), so their gamma values differ. Neither
has been tuned. Later tuning needs match-grouped folds within training data;
the held-out test matches should not guide parameter choices.

The package's built-in probability estimation uses internal cross-validation
that does not enforce match groups. It stays within the training data, but its
probability calibration is preliminary because rallies from a match are related.
Also, fitting here weights rally snapshots equally; the evaluation above gives
sets equal weight. The class predictions shown earlier come from the SVM decision
rule and need not match a 0.5 threshold on the estimated probabilities.
